memo.thesis_en: We own three shares of Accenture, bought a day ago at $251.845, and they are down 3.55% since. That is noise, and a price decline is never a reason to sell a business whose economics are intact. The snapshot shows a 5-year average ROE of 26.9% and debt-to-equity of 0.32. It also shows a reported margin of safety of 45.5% against an owner-earnings DCF value of $437.57 a share, though that DCF leans on an 8% growth cap and a 5% discount rate. My doubt is the moat: switching costs in consulting are real but softer than Coca-Cola's brand, and a services business that must keep rebuilding its edge against technological change is not a franchise I can underwrite for decades. So I keep the position, I don't add to it yet, and I'd want to read the earnings history and management record before I got excited.

But I've learned that a cheap price on a business I can't confidently see ten years out is a trap, and it is the kind of mistake Charlie and I made with Dexter Shoe. This looks like a services and outsourcing business, where the work can be repriced or automated away, and I can't point to a moat that would hold up for a decade. The snapshot also gives me no ten-year earnings record and nothing on management, so those tests were not met. I'll pass and wait for a pitch squarely in my sweet spot.

Price declines don't trigger a sale; moat erosion does, and nothing in this snapshot shows that. The owner-earnings DCF says $363 a share against a $106.96 price, but that rests on 8% growth and a 5% discount rate, and I wouldn't bet the farm on a number that generous. My real worry is that apparel can be fashion-driven, and fashion-driven brands must be rebuilt every few years, so I can't extend full conviction. I'll keep the shares, own them for the business and not the quote, and add only if I can confirm the brand's pricing power still holds.

memo.thesis_en: I don't own Adobe, and the numbers on the page are tempting: a 5-year average ROE of 40.0%, debt-to-equity of 0.41, and a price of $236.96 against a DCF value of $467.50, which is a 49.3% margin of safety. Creative software is an industry where the tools themselves may be rebuilt by new technology, and a moat that has to be rebuilt continuously is no moat at all. The snapshot also doesn't give me ten years of earnings history, management tenure, ROIC or the Treasury yield, so I can't finish my homework. I'll keep it on the list and wait for evidence that the switching costs hold, rather than buy on a cheap-looking number.

The economics rest on how embedded the products become in professional work: once teams, templates and habits are built around a toolset, leaving is costly. The risk is that new technology changes how content is created and lowers the barrier for rivals. The snapshot gives me the valuation and return figures but not the segment or retention detail, so my description of the business is general.

memo.thesis_en: I own this one, and the numbers I can see give me no reason to sell. The snapshot shows a 5-year average ROE of 23.8%, debt-to-equity of 0.40, and a price about 18% under an owner-earnings value of $260 per share, built on zero assumed growth. I do not call this a wonderful business. A car dealer's moat is thinner than a candy maker's, and it rests mostly on franchise protections, so I hold it with moderate confidence rather than conviction. The shares are down about 2% since August, which means nothing to me; a price decline with the thesis intact is not a sell signal. I will keep what I own, but I need evidence on earnings consistency and management before I add to it.

The snapshot shows a five-year average ROE of 23.66% and debt-to-equity of 0.37, with the stock at $64.32 against a model value of $98.59, a 35.51% margin of safety. I want to be honest about the gaps: the snapshot doesn't give me ten years of earnings, CEO tenure or insider activity, and the model leans on 8% growth and a 5% discount rate, which is generous. So I keep what I own, don't add on faith, and let time work.

memo.thesis_en: I own this one, and the question is whether to keep it, not whether to buy it. The snapshot shows a 5-year average ROE of 29.3%, debt-to-equity reported at 0.0, and a market cap near $6.0 billion. The owner-earnings model gives $169.13 a share against a $54.22 price, a 67.9% margin of safety. That gap is so wide that I distrust the model, which uses a 5% discount rate and 8% growth. Even so, I'd rather own a copper tube and fittings maker with this return on equity than sell it after 12 days, with the position essentially flat at -0.12%. The gaps are real: the snapshot gives no 10-year earnings record, no management tenure, and no moat evidence beyond the returns. memo.thesis_en: I don't own this one, and I'm not ready to. A builder of warships for a single customer, the U.S. Navy, has a real barrier to entry, because almost nobody else can build these vessels. But a barrier to entry is not the same as pricing power. When your one buyer sets the terms, the moat protects your existence more than it protects your returns. The model shows a wide discount, price near $297 against about $559 of estimated value, but that value leans on 8% growth and a 5% discount rate, and I distrust a margin of safety that comes mostly from generous assumptions. Five-year average ROE of 15.3% and debt-to-equity of 0.49 clear my bars by a whisker, not comfortably. I also can't verify ten years of earnings, CEO tenure, or the Treasury yield from this snapshot, so I'll wait.

memo.moat_analysis: The moat is regulatory and intangible: few facilities and workforces in the country can build large nuclear-powered naval vessels, and a new entrant would face enormous capital, security, and qualification hurdles. That supports durability, since the Navy needs a domestic industrial base. The weakness is that the sole customer is a monopsony. It can cap margins, dictate contract terms, and push cost overruns back onto the builder. The snapshot's 5-year average ROE of 15.26%, barely above my 15% hurdle, suggests the moat yields adequate returns, not exceptional ones. This is a toll bridge with one customer who sets the toll.

Huntington Ingalls is a shipbuilder and defense contractor. It designs, builds, overhauls, and maintains naval vessels, mainly for the U.S. Navy and Coast Guard, including nuclear-powered ships and amphibious and surface combatants. It also sells technical and mission-support services to government customers.

It earns money through long-term government contracts, often cost-plus or fixed-price, with revenue recognized as work progresses and profit tied to execution against cost and schedule. Capital needs are heavy and returns depend on labor productivity, supply chain reliability, and budget appropriations. Demand is visible years ahead, but pricing is negotiated with one dominant buyer.
